transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-30 16:00 PDT | Duration approx 58m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Maya Ortiz (Redwood) — Samir Patel, Lina Gomez, Omar Reed, Julia Tan (Quantica Labs)

Summary: Quick deep dive into throughput guardrails. Walkthrough of scheduler knobs and a proposed adaptive prefetch/traffic-shaping approach. Agree to run an 8-GPU bench and exchange traces.

[00:00:00] Alex Chen: okay everyone thanks for joining, um we're gonna focus on throughput guardrails, continuous batching and a few knobs that we usually tweak when customers have peaky workloads. Maya will lead the bench plan. Samir — quick note, thanks for sharing the traffic doc ahead of time.
[00:00:20] Samir Patel: yeah thanks, I was hoping we could also talk about doing this inside our VPC-onprem setup — we have strict egress and KMS requirements.
[00:00:30] Maya Ortiz: great, we'll cover onprem constraints. Quick, can you confirm the SLOs — the product team said p95 < 250ms for <512 tokens and cost target of X tokens per thousand? Julia, is that right?
[00:00:42] Julia Tan: correct, p95 <250ms for short responses; budget target is kind of soft but we want to avoid order-of-magnitude jumps in token cost.
[00:00:50] Lina Gomez: and we have a mix of 1- to 1024-token seqs, heavy tail, about 6% are >512, 1% >1024.
[00:01:02] Maya Ortiz: perfect that's useful. Okay, high-level: continuous batching helps pack requests and maximize throughput, but with peaky arrival you need guardrails — max_num_seqs, token_ceiling, and an adaptive prefetch policy that warms KV cache only for sequences likely to be used.
[00:01:20] Alex Chen: to add, our traffic-shaper idea does token smoothing — essentially we shape bursty arrivals to a controlled rate to avoid thrashing the scheduler and cold-kv penalty.
[00:01:30] Omar Reed: is token smoothing just delaying requests? we can't add too much latency.
[00:01:36] Maya Ortiz: good question. It's adaptive and uses a tiny headroom window — like a 50–150ms slack — we try micro-batching in that window, if latency is tight we fall back to immediate dispatch. Empirically it buys better KV hitrates and larger effective batch sizes without visible added tail.
[00:01:58] Samir Patel: sounds promising. Can you walk through specific knobs you recommend? max_num_seqs, token limits, eviction policies — we're especially worried about worst-case p99.
[00:02:10] Maya Ortiz: sure — default progression we use for peaky LLM workloads: 1) set max_num_seqs to 6–8 for short models (8 gives good packing); 2) configure token_ceiling per request class — for customer short responses set token_ceiling 512, for long responses allow 1024 but throttle concurrency; 3) implement a prefetch_profile where we prefetch only top-K prefixes based on recent traffic — that reduces unnecessary KV warming.
[00:02:36] Lina Gomez: wait top-K prefixes — how do you detect that? our prompts are highly dynamic.
[00:02:42] Maya Ortiz: we do a lightweight prefix frequency estimator over a sliding window (anonymized hashes) — even dynamic prompts have repeated prefixes like system instructions, user prompts templates, etc. It's not perfect but hitrate improves significantly.
[00:02:56] Alex Chen: also quantization helps reduce GPU mem pressure and increase throughput — int8/llm.int8 modes can increase throughput 1.4–2x on some models, but watch the KV cache layout; with quant you might need different kernel selection.
[00:03:12] Samir Patel: do we lose quality? for our product even small hallucination rate changes are important.
[00:03:18] Maya Ortiz: there is a tradeoff. For many instruction-style completions int8 is fine, but we recommend running a small eval set — Redwood Optimize can run prompt evals and flag regressions.
[00:03:28] Julia Tan: sorry quick interruption, regulatory team requires KMS with HSM and onprem logs. Can your prefetching run entirely inside our VPC?
[00:03:36] Alex Chen: yes, Redwood Private supports prefetching inside the customer's VPC and HSM integration; you keep control of keys and logs, we only provide the orchestration. We'll send the Private deployment docs after call.
[00:03:48] Omar Reed: good. about eviction — when the KV cache is under pressure what's recommended? LRU? TTL?
[00:03:54] Maya Ortiz: we typically use a two-tier eviction: frequency-weighted LRU plus a small protected set for very hot prefixes (pinned for short windows). That avoids repeated re-warm. You can also reserve a prefetch budget per customer shard to avoid noisy neighbors.
[00:04:12] Samir Patel: what about max_num_seqs interacting with fairness across customers? we have multiple internal tenants.
[00:04:18] Maya Ortiz: you can set per-tenant max_num_seqs and soft-priorities. Redwood's scheduler supports weighted fair-share windows; when a tenant hits max_num_seqs we degrade to token_ceiling enforcement and apply priority decay to produce fairness without starvation.
[00:04:34] Alex Chen: quick bench numbers we've seen: with continuous batching + adaptive prefetch, effective throughput can increase 35–60% for peaky workloads while p95 latency improves 10–20% due to higher KV hitrates. But numbers vary with seq distribution and model size.
[00:04:52] Lina Gomez: those are promising. can we see an example config you would suggest for our workload?
[00:04:58] Maya Ortiz: yes — we'll propose: max_num_seqs=8 for short model; token_ceiling=512 for route A, 1024 for route B; prefetch_profile=windowed-topk with k=200 and decay 30m; kv_protected_set=top50 prefixes pinned for 60s; eviction=freq-lru. We'll put exact settings in the deck.
[00:05:20] Samir Patel: about token smoothing — any prebuilt policies? we don't want to write custom rate limiter glue.
[00:05:26] Alex Chen: Redwood ships built-in traffic shapers: micro-batch window (ms), smoothing target rate, and overload fallback (immediate dispatch or degraded model). You configure them per-route in the Console.
[00:05:40] Omar Reed: okay but if we add smoothing won't our p99 jump? we need p99 guarantees for certain endpoints.
[00:05:46] Maya Ortiz: we recommend tiered routing: critical endpoints bypass smoothing and go to reserved capacity (Dedicated) or higher priority lanes. Non-critical can route through adaptive smoothing. That way p99 guarantees remain.
[00:05:58] Julia Tan: can Redwood run the bench inside our VPC or do you need host access?
[00:06:04] Alex Chen: pilot can run in two ways: 1) Redwood-managed hosted pilot with an anonymized trace you provide and our regional infra, or 2) Redwood Private pilot in your VPC where our SE runs bench inside your environment. For security-sensitive customers we prefer option 2.
[00:06:18] Samir Patel: we prefer option 2. what's the timeline?
[00:06:22] Maya Ortiz: if you share the trace and approve the pilot contract we can do bench within a week — SE bench run ~2–3 days plus analysis. We'll need sample tokens and a short eval set.
[00:06:34] Alex Chen: also we'll attach suggested quantization profiles to try int8 on a dev branch and compare output quality with Redwood Optimize.
[00:06:42] Lina Gomez: good. can you explain in plain terms how prefetch avoids warming everything?
[00:06:48] Maya Ortiz: think of prefetch as probabilistic warm: we score prefixes by recent frequency + expected reuse and only warm the top fraction that fit within prefetch_budget. Budget is expressed in prefix tokens per second so you don't exceed memory or IO. Unobserved prefixes are loaded on demand; hot ones stay warm.
[00:07:06] Samir Patel: is there instrumentation we can see live? we need KV hitrate, prefix churn, batch sizes over time.
[00:07:12] Alex Chen: Console exposes per-route KV hitrate, avg batch size, seq packing efficiency, and token-level cost. We'll provide a dashboard template for Quantica's pilot.
[00:07:22] Omar Reed: what about backpressure — if the GPU gets saturated will requests queue indefinitely?
[00:07:28] Maya Ortiz: scheduler enforces token_caps and max_queue_depth. You can configure graceful fallback: either reject with 429, route to a smaller model, or queue with a timeout. We usually recommend queue timeout + fallback to a cheaper model for non-critical workloads.
[00:07:44] Julia Tan: any gotchas with onprem SGX or unusual KMS setups?
[00:07:50] Alex Chen: HSM integration is supported but adds ~10–20ms to key ops in some setups; we cache decrypted keys inside a secure enclave to reduce frequent HSM calls. We'll surface this in the Private docs.
[00:07:58] Samir Patel: great. can you share an example of the bench script you'll run? we want to inspect it.
[00:08:04] Maya Ortiz: yes — it's a k6-based driver that replays anonymized traces, varies seq length by sampled histogram, measures p50/p95/p99 and KV hitrate. We'll share the repo link.
[00:08:14] Alex Chen: next let's walk through a quick failure scenario: burst arrives that exceeds prefetch budget and cache thrashes — how we recover.
[00:08:22] Maya Ortiz: two layers: immediate eviction control plus token smoothing. If thrash detected (KV miss spike and p95 increases), we temporarily increase token_ceiling to allow more packs and enable aggressive preemptive pinning for top prefixes. Also automatically route some traffic to a lower-capacity lane or model to stabilize.
[00:08:42] Lina Gomez: that dynamic pinning concerns me — can it create cache contention?
[00:08:46] Maya Ortiz: it's risk-managed: pin windows are short, pinned set size small, and we only pin when hitrate benefit outweighs eviction cost based on heuristics. We'll tune with your traffic during pilot.
[00:08:58] Samir Patel: ok makes sense. Can we get an initial config by Monday?
[00:09:03] Alex Chen: yes we'll have a recommended config and bench plan by 2026-07-01.
[00:09:10] Julia Tan: outstanding items for us — provide the trace and decide VPC pilot host.
[00:09:15] Alex Chen: noted. Anything else?
[00:09:19] Samir Patel: one more — costs. how do token smoothing and pinning affect unit cost?
[00:09:24] Maya Ortiz: effective cost per token usually drops because we increase batch efficiency and reduce repeated re-computation (less cold-start and fewer kv misses). Pinning uses memory but that's minor compared to saved compute. We'll produce a cost projection in the bench report.
[00:09:40] Alex Chen: cool — wrap up: Redwood will run bench, send Private deployment docs + security pack, and propose knobs. Quantica to share trace and confirm pilot window. We'll follow up with timeline and JIRA. Thanks all.
[00:09:56] Samir Patel: thanks, really helpful.

Notes: occasional transcription errors present — some product names may be abbreviated. References shared: pilot contract template (link in email), Private deployment guide (will be attached), bench repo (link to be provided).

End of transcript.
